pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Sunlight warms things up

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, England):** no KS1 'energy' content (energy enters at KS3), so no direct UK statutory match; the honest UK home is KS1 'Working scientifically' (observing closely, performing simple tests, gathering and recording data) and the Year-1 'Seasonal changes' unit (observe weather/day-length across seasons).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** NATIONAL (NGSS): K-PS3-1 (verbatim) '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-1]'; clarification examples — sand, soil, rocks, water; assessment boundary — temperature limited to RELATIVE measures (warmer/cooler). NGSS-anchored.

- **Operational details:** Children make firsthand observations that sunlight WARMS Earth's surface: ground, water, rocks and objects in the sun feel warmer than the same things in the shade. Strictly RELATIVE and sensory (warmer/cooler by touch, or a simple thermometer) — NO degrees, no mechanism, no light-vs-heat theory; the win is the observed cause: sun on a surface → it warms up. This observation feeds 'Building shade from the sun' (reduce that warming) and, much later, Sun-driven weather.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, age 5-6, pre-readers).
bestPractices: Lead with firsthand sensory observation: have children touch surfaces in sun vs shade — sunny tarmac vs shaded grass, a sunny windowsill vs a shaded one — and say which feels warmer; the felt contrast IS the evidence.
Hold the comparison fair without naming it: same object/surface, two spots (one sunny, one shaded), at the same time — so 'the sun' is the only difference.
Move from touch to a simple relative thermometer or colour-change strip to confirm warmer/cooler, but keep it relative — the assessment boundary excludes degrees at this age.
Use a leave-and-revisit investigation: put two identical cups of water (or rocks) in sun and shade, predict, then check later — building the sun-as-source-of-warmth idea over time.
Name the source plainly in talk: 'the Sun warms it up; in the shade the sun can't reach, so it stays cooler' — framing shade as blocking the sun, not as a maker of cold.
keyRepresentations: Paired sun/shade comparison of the SAME object (sunny rock vs shaded rock) — the canonical observation.
Touch/feel as the primary instrument, backed by a simple relative thermometer or a colour-changing temperature strip.
A sun-as-source picture: rays reaching the ground/water/objects and warming them.
Across-the-day anchor: cool ground in the morning → warm by midday → cooler again in shade/evening.
commonMisconceptions: 'Shade makes things cold' — rather than shade simply blocking the sun so the area doesn't get warmed; the cool is the absence of warming, not a cold source.
Thinking everything in the sun is equally warm — dark/heavier things warm more (a real effect, kept as enrichment, not the core claim).
Conflating the sun's LIGHT and its WARMTH, or believing only light (not warmth) reaches us — here the focus is the warming effect.
'Things stay warm by themselves' — not noticing that without the sun (shade, night) surfaces cool down again.
Believing sunlight can't warm water or see-through things — water and clear objects in the sun warm too.

learn.summary: For ages 5-6: children observe that sunlight warms Earth's surfaces — ground, water, rocks and objects in the sun feel warmer than the same things in the shade. Learning is strictly relative and sensory (warmer/cooler by touch or a simple relative thermometer or colour strip), with no degrees, no mechanism and no light-vs-heat theory. The core win is the observed cause: sun reaching a surface warms it; shade is cooler because it blocks the sun's warmth, not because it sends out cold. Firsthand outdoor observation is the heart of this objective; screen activities rehearse the cause and prediction and should accompany, not replace, real touching and leaving-and-revisiting.

activities.title: Touch the sun, touch the shade (firsthand outdoor observation)
feedback: If the child says the shade 'makes it cold', feel both spots together, then move the shaded object into the sun and wait: it warms up, showing there is no cold source — only more or less of the sun's warmth.

If a child thinks the Sun only warms things in summer and 'isn't hot' on a cold or winter day, compare a sunny spot with a shady spot of the same surface on a cold day using touch or a relative thermometer — a surface that has been in the sun for a while usually feels warmer, even if the difference is small.
Affirm the felt contrast as the evidence: 'the sunny one felt warmer, and that warmth came from the Sun.'
activities.rationale: The standard's practice is literally to make firsthand observations, and the concept is a felt one — warm sun-baked surfaces against cool shaded ones. Holding object and time constant isolates the sun as the only difference. Framing shade as blocking the sun (not making cold), and showing the cold-day sun still warms, targets the common misconceptions directly.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-1 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-1]'); clarification examples sand/soil/rocks/water; assessment boundary limits temperature to relative measures (warmer/cooler).
Young children commonly think shade 'makes cold' rather than blocking the sun's warming, and conflate the sun's light with its warmth.
learnerActions: Go outside and touch the same kind of surface in two spots — e.g. sunny tarmac vs shaded tarmac, sunny grass vs shaded grass, or a sunny windowsill vs a shaded one — and say which feels warmer.
Keep the comparison fair: same object or surface, two spots (one sunny, one shaded), checked at the same time, so the sun is the only difference.
After touching, confirm warmer/cooler with a simple relative thermometer or colour-changing temperature strip if available — staying relative, never reading out degrees.
Say in plain words what was felt: 'the Sun warms it up; in the shade the sun can't reach it, so it stays cooler.'
activities.intendedInsight: Sunlight reaching a surface warms it; a shaded spot is cooler because the sun's warmth is blocked, not because shade makes cold.

activities.title: Leave and revisit: two cups in sun and shade
feedback: If a child says the shady cup will get colder because the shade makes cold, that signals the 'shade makes cold' idea — revisit by feeling both and moving the shady cup into the sun, then checking again later to find it has warmed.
If a child expects the sunny cup to feel the same straight away as after a long wait, point to the leave-and-revisit checks: after sitting in the sun for a while, it got warmer than it was at first.
Praise prediction-then-check: 'you said the sunny one would be warmer, and we checked — that's how scientists find out.'
activities.rationale: A leave-and-revisit investigation builds the sun-as-source idea over time and makes prediction a diagnostic moment: the stated reason distinguishes 'sun warms' from 'shade makes cold', and the repeated check surfaces the 'warmth doesn't build up' misconception.
sourceClaims: K-PS3-1 verbatim ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS3-1]'); clarification examples sand/soil/rocks/water; assessment boundary limits temperature to relative measures (warmer/cooler).
learnerActions: Put two identical cups of water filled from the same jug (or two matching rocks), so they start out equally warm, outside — one in full sun, one in shade.
Before leaving them, predict which will be warmer later and say why.
Return after a while and compare with hands or a relative thermometer; talk about what changed and whether the prediction held.
Optionally revisit the same sunny spot after a short time and again a little later to notice warmth can build up the longer it sits in the sun.
activities.intendedInsight: The sun is the source of the extra warmth that builds up over time; the shaded item stays cooler than the sunny one because the sun's warmth does not reach it.

activities.title: Sunny-day sandbox (on-screen cause-and-prediction rehearsal)
feedback: All prompts picture-and-audio for pre-readers; use warmer/cooler faces or words, never degrees.

When a prediction matches the meter, confirm the rule: 'the sun reached it, so it got warmer.' When the cloud covers the sun, name it: 'the sun is blocked, so it stops warming and starts to cool' — and remember that on screen this happens fast, while a real warm surface would cool more slowly.
Treat the sandbox as a rehearsal of the cause, then take the idea outdoors where the warmth can actually be felt.
activities.rationale: A draggable sandbox with a live warm/cool meter, colour glow, and a movable cloud/umbrella lets a 5-6-year-old act out the causal rule and do predict-then-check. It is proposed as a useful on-screen rehearsal of the cause, but it is a simplified model and cannot deliver the felt warmth that is central to the objective, so it should accompany real outdoor observation, not substitute for it.
learnerActions: Drag an object (a rock, a cup of water, a metal slide, sand) between a sunny patch and a shaded patch on screen.
Watch a simple warm/cool meter and a colour or glow cue respond live as the object moves into the sun or into the shade.

Slide a cloud or umbrella over the sun and watch the modelled scene cool — noting this is a simplified model that cools quickly, whereas a real warm surface would cool gradually once the sun is blocked.
Before moving an object, predict out loud whether it will get warmer or cooler, then move it and check.
activities.intendedInsight: You control the warmth by controlling whether the sun reaches the object — sun on it = warmer, blocked = cooler — and you can predict the result before acting.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal sunny scene (reference observation)
feedback: Keep language relative (warm/cool) and tie every reveal back to whether the sun reaches that object.
Use as a companion for naming and reinforcing, alongside firsthand touching.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal scene delivers the sun-as-source naming cleanly for pre-readers with picture+audio. It names and reinforces the idea but does not host the predict-then-check action or real observation, so it works as a reference companion rather than the main investigation.
learnerActions: In a single sunny outdoor scene, tap the rock, the puddle, the slide or the shaded bench.
Hear which is 'warm — the sun is shining on it' or 'cool — it's in the shade' with picture-and-audio.
Tap a flap on the sun that says 'I warm things up.'
activities.intendedInsight: Objects the sun shines on are warmer; objects in shade are cooler because the sun is blocked.

activities.title: Which feels warmer? (sorting check)
feedback: This checks a conclusion more than it builds the observation, so pair it with firsthand work; at this age it leans on adult or audio support.
A sort can check that a child classifies sun/shade correctly, but it does not itself elicit the felt observation or an explanation — follow it with real touching.
If a child says water or clear objects can't be warmed by the sun, revisit with a real cup of water left in the sun — it warms too.
activities.rationale: A picture+audio categorisation can confirm whether the idea has landed and surface misconceptions (e.g. that sunlight can't warm water or transparent things), but it tests classification rather than building the firsthand observation at the centre of the standard.
sourceClaims: Young children commonly think shade 'makes cold' rather than blocking the sun's warming, and conflate the sun's light with its warmth.
learnerActions: Sort pictured objects into 'in the sun = warmer' vs 'in the shade = cooler' using picture-and-audio.
Answer a 'which feels warmer?' picture choice using relative language only.
Try tricky cases: a clear cup of water or a see-through object in the sun also warms up.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can apply the sun-warms / shade-cooler rule to new objects, including water and clear things.

constraints: Keep all temperature talk RELATIVE (warmer/cooler by touch, simple thermometer, or colour strip): no degrees, no mechanism, no light-vs-heat theory at age 5-6 — this matches the assessment boundary.

Firsthand sensory observation is the objective itself; on-screen sandbox, tap-to-reveal, and sorting activities are scaffolds that rehearse the cause or check the conclusion and must not replace real outdoor touching and leaving-and-revisiting.
Frame shade as blocking the sun's warmth, not as a maker of cold; avoid any language implying cold is a substance that is sent out.
Hold comparisons fair: same object/surface, two spots, same time, so the sun is the only difference.

The tap-to-reveal scene reinforces and names the idea but does not support predict-then-check; the sorting check tests classification and leans on adult/audio support rather than building the observation.

Enrichment only (not the core claim): dark-coloured surfaces, and some materials (e.g. a metal slide vs a patch of grass), can feel warmer in the sun than lighter ones — keep this as an optional extension, not a requirement. Do NOT teach that 'heavier things warm more'.
If observing shade or a cover, look at the cool patch and the shadow it casts on the ground — never ask a child to look at the Sun through a cover or hold material up toward the Sun.

The sandbox is a simplified model; blocking the sun cools the modelled scene quickly, whereas a real warm surface cools gradually once the sun is blocked — do not present the model's instant cooling as a real-world prediction.
UK note: there is no KS1 statutory 'energy' content in England; the honest home is KS1 Working Scientifically and the Year-1 Seasonal changes unit. The specific standard anchor is US NGSS K-PS3-1.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source legacy framing that 'no digital artefact can deliver that bodily sensation' and that 3D 'adds no conceptual gain' was softened: the screen sandbox is scoped as a complement to firsthand observation with a stated affordance/limit, not as proof that screens cannot teach or that 3D is universally worthless.

The source claim about children's misconceptions (IOP Spark) is marked verified:false in the row; treat the 'shade makes cold' and light-vs-warmth conflation framing as plausible but not independently confirmed here.

The assessment errorPattern 'Sun only warms in summer / isn't hot in winter' carries reteachPrerequisiteId mt_go5i87u2b9; it is reinstated as feedback in the firsthand activity with a cold-day comparison, and reteach should route to that prerequisite micro-topic if the child denies winter warming.

The original row's enrichment wording 'dark/heavier things warm more' was corrected: greater mass warms more slowly (more thermal mass); the reliable effect is colour/material, so the guidance teaches darker/material differences and drops 'heavier'. Confirm any comparison with an adult-supervised check if used.

The sandbox sourceClaims were set to [] because K-PS3-1 concerns firsthand observation, which the simulation explicitly cannot deliver; it is not a direct source for a screen-based method. The same applies to the tap-to-reveal reference scene.
The assessment row's diagnostic (two-cup predict-then-measure, reasoning tier) was preserved as the leave-and-revisit activity's prediction step; assessment fields themselves were not modified.

assess.poeTask: Put two identical cups of water (or two thermometers) out on a sunny day — one in full sun, one in shade. FIRST ask the child which will be warmer after ten minutes AND why. The reason is the diagnostic part: a 'shade makes cold' child predicts the shady one gets actively colder, while a 'sun warms' child predicts the sunny one rises and the shady one barely changes. Then measure and compare.
probeDeeper: If we move the shady bench out into the sunshine and wait, what will happen to how it feels — and why?
At night there's no sun at all. Is that because something is making cold, or because the sun's warmth has gone away?
Which will get warmer left in the sun: a metal slide or a patch of grass? How could we find out?
Where's the best place to leave a cup of water to warm it up, and where to keep it cool? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: The shady bench is cooler because the tree blocks the sun's light and warmth from reaching it — the sun isn't warming it up. The shade doesn't make cold or send out coldness; 'cooler' just means less of the sun's warming got there.

errorPatterns.pattern: The shade (or the cold) actively makes things cold, as if cold were a substance that comes out ('the shade sends cold onto the bench').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Feel both benches, then move the shady one into the sun and watch it warm; there is no 'cold source', only more or less of the sun's warmth.
errorPatterns.distractor: The shade makes cold and sends it onto the bench.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says shade produces or sends cold rather than blocking warmth.

errorPatterns.pattern: The Sun only warms things in summer / the Sun isn't hot in winter ('no warming from winter sun').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Compare a sunny spot with a shady spot on a cold day using a thermometer — the sunny surface is still warmer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies that the sun warms surfaces on a cold or winter day.

errorPatterns.pattern: Everything in the sun is the same warmth and warmth doesn't build up over time ('it's just warm or not').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Measure the same sunny spot after 5 minutes and after 15 minutes and compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't expect a surface to get warmer the longer it sits in the sun.

responseLevels.gap: Says the shade or the cold makes or sends cold; treats cold as a thing rather than as less warmth.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the sun warms surfaces and shade is cooler because it blocks that warmth (no cold source), and predicts a new case — moving an object into or out of the sun, or which surface warms more.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the sunny spot is warmer and the shady one cooler, but explains it as the shade 'making it cold' rather than blocking the sun's warmth.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: On a sunny day the bench in the sun feels warm but the bench under the tree feels cooler. A friend says 'the shade makes it cold.' Do you agree — what is really making the shady bench cooler?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks 'cold is a thing' says the shade actively makes or sends cold — different from one who says the shade simply blocks the sun's warmth. The reason tier separates 'shade makes cold' from 'shade blocks the sun's heat'.
